subproblems.natural_proof:
Provenance and scope. This is Lemma IE of the parent-supplied proof (Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 5, estimates 3.2–3.4, "standard estimates for harmonic functions (which follow directly from the mean-value property)"), made self-contained by proving in full, as Part 1, the mean value property (the parent's Lemma MV) on which it relies. The statement and its frozen Lean type are character-identical to the comparator-accepted DAG node root.density_one_implies_regular-a1.epsilon_regularity-a1.allard_graph-a1.harmonic_approximation-a1.interior_estimates-a1 (Submission.dorag_ha_interior_estimates, candidate 3853ad1ff1a11a7855f6e8df2d2f252bc76c23a4). Apart from this preamble and the Part headings, the text below reproduces the parent's Lemmas MV and IE verbatim. It uses only theorems of the pinned Mathlib, cited by name, and no DAG declaration.

Global conventions.
- n ≥ 1 and ℝⁿ = Euclid n, with Euclidean norm |·| = ‖·‖ and inner product ⟨·,·⟩; Lⁿ := volume.
- B̆_ρ(y) is the open ball (Lean ball y ρ) and closedBall(y, ρ) the closed ball; B_ρ := B̆_ρ(0) unless a lemma fixes another meaning.
- e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1.
- For f differentiable at z: Df(z) := fderiv ℝ f z, whose operator norm ‖Df(z)‖ is the Euclidean length of the gradient ∇f(z), and ∂_if := Df(·)e_i.
- For f of class C² on an open set V and z ∈ V: D²f(z)(a, b) := iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 f z ![a, b] = D(Df)(z)(a)(b) (iteratedFDeriv_two_apply), and Δf(z) := Σ_i D²f(z)(e_i, e_i).
- "h is harmonic on V" means that h is C^m on V for every m ∈ ℕ and Δh = 0 on V.
- For Lipschitz u and C¹ ζ: ∇u·∇ζ := Σ_i Du(e_i)Dζ(e_i). This is exactly the Lean integrand Σ_i fderiv ℝ u v (e_i) * fderiv ℝ ζ v (e_i).
Each lemma below may fix further local notation, valid only inside that lemma.

Part 1 (Lemma MV, the mean value property; proved in full here and used in Part 2).
Lemma MV (mean value property). Let n ≥ 1, let U ⊆ ℝⁿ (= Euclid n) be open, and let h : ℝⁿ → ℝ be of class C² on U with Δh(y) := Σ_{i<n} D²h(y)(e_i, e_i) = 0 for every y ∈ U, where D²h(y)(a, b) = iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 h y ![a, b] and e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1. Let x ∈ ℝⁿ and r > 0 with closedBall(x, r) ⊆ U. Then (i) for every continuous g : ℝ → ℝ with g(t) = 0 for all t ≥ r², ∫_{ℝⁿ} h(x − y)·g(|y|²) dy = h(x)·∫_{ℝⁿ} g(|y|²) dy; and (ii) ∫_{B̆_r(x)} h = Lⁿ(B̆_r(x))·h(x), where Lⁿ = volume is Lebesgue measure, B̆_r(x) is the open ball and the measure is taken as a real number (ENNReal.toReal).
Proof of Lemma MV.
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 5, 3.2–3.4 calls these "standard estimates for harmonic functions (which follow directly from the mean-value property)"; cf. Evans, PDE, §2.2.2, and Gilbarg–Trudinger, Thm 2.1. The proof below uses neither surface measure nor the divergence theorem. It needs only differentiation under the integral sign and integration by parts for compactly supported C¹ (hence Lipschitz) functions. Mathlib's only mean value theorem for harmonic functions is for ℂ (Analysis/Complex/Harmonic/MeanValue.lean), so a general-n proof is required.

Conventions.
- |·| and ⟨·,·⟩ are the Euclidean norm and inner product on ℝⁿ = Euclid n, and Lⁿ = volume.
- For f differentiable at z: Df(z) = fderiv ℝ f z; ∇f(z) is the vector with Df(z)v = ⟨∇f(z), v⟩; ∂_if := Df(·)e_i.
- If f is C² on an open set V and z ∈ V, then iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 f z ![a, b] = D(Df)(z)(a)(b) =: D²f(z)(a, b) (iteratedFDeriv_two_apply), and Δf(z) := Σ_i D²f(z)(e_i, e_i). Since V is open, these are the classical derivatives.

1. (Room around the ball.) closedBall(x, r) is compact and lies in the open set U. So there is η > 0 with closedBall(x, r + η) ⊆ U (IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open and cthickening_closedBall). Put r' := r + η. Since h is C² on U, h and Dh are continuous on the compact set closedBall(x, r'). Let A₀ := sup|h| and A₁ := sup‖Dh‖ over closedBall(x, r'); both are finite.

2. (A radial potential.) Fix a continuous g : ℝ → ℝ with g(t) = 0 for t ≥ r², and let γ := sup_{0 ≤ t ≤ r²}|g(t)|.
- Put P(t) := ½∫_{r²}^{t} g(τ) dτ. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, P is C¹ with P' = g/2. Also P(t) = 0 for t ≥ r², since g vanishes on [r², t].
- Put Ψ(y) := P(|y|²). Then Ψ is C¹ on ℝⁿ with DΨ(y)v = 2P'(|y|²)⟨y, v⟩, i.e. ∇Ψ(y) = g(|y|²)·y.
- If |y| ≥ r then Ψ(y) = 0 and ∇Ψ(y) = 0. So Ψ is C¹ with compact support in closedBall(0, r), and in particular Lipschitz (ContDiff.lipschitzWith_of_hasCompactSupport).

3. (The function M and its derivative.) Let κ := r'/r > 1 and I := (1 − κ, κ), an open interval containing [0, 1]. For s ∈ I and |y| ≤ r we have |sy| < κr = r', so x − sy ∈ closedBall(x, r') ⊆ U. Define F(s, y) := h(x − sy)·g(|y|²) and M(s) := ∫_{ℝⁿ} F(s, y) dy for s ∈ I.
- If |y| ≥ r then g(|y|²) = 0, so F(s, y) = 0 whatever h(x − sy) is. Thus F(s, ·) is the extension by zero of a function continuous on closedBall(0, r). It is measurable, satisfies |F(s, y)| ≤ A₀γ·1_{closedBall(0,r)}(y), and is integrable.
- For |y| ≤ r, s ↦ F(s, y) is differentiable on I with derivative −Dh(x − sy)(y)·g(|y|²), by the chain rule (h is differentiable on U). For |y| ≥ r it is identically 0, with derivative 0.
- In every case the derivative is bounded by A₁rγ·1_{closedBall(0,r)}(y), which is integrable and independent of s.
By differentiation under the integral sign (hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le), M is differentiable on I with M'(s) = −∫ Dh(x − sy)(y)·g(|y|²) dy, the integrand being 0 for |y| ≥ r. In particular M is continuous on [0, 1].

4. (M' = 0 on (0, 1].) Fix s ∈ (0, 1] and let G(y) := h(x − sy).
- For y in the open ball V := B̆_{r'}(0) we have |sy| < r', so x − sy ∈ closedBall(x, r') ⊆ U. Hence G is C² on V with DG(y) = −s·Dh(x − sy) and D²G(y)(a, b) = s²·D²h(x − sy)(a, b). So ΔG(y) = s²·Δh(x − sy) = 0 for y ∈ V.
- Choose χ ∈ C^∞(ℝⁿ) with χ ≡ 1 on B̆_{r+η/3}(0) and tsupport χ = closedBall(0, r + 2η/3) ⊆ V: a ContDiffBump centred at 0 with rIn = r + η/3 and rOut = r + 2η/3 (ContDiffBump.tsupport_eq). B̆_{r+η/3}(0) is an open neighbourhood of closedBall(0, r).
- For each i let φ_i := χ·∂_iG on V and φ_i := 0 off V. Then φ_i is C¹ on ℝⁿ: ∂_iG is C¹ on V, φ_i vanishes on the open set ℝⁿ ∖ tsupport χ, and these two open sets cover ℝⁿ. φ_i has compact support, hence is Lipschitz.
- By LipschitzWith.integral_lineDeriv_mul_eq with f := Ψ, g := φ_i, v := e_i:
  ∫ lineDeriv ℝ Ψ y e_i · φ_i(y) dy = ∫ lineDeriv ℝ φ_i y (−e_i) · Ψ(y) dy.
  Both functions are differentiable everywhere, so lineDeriv ℝ Ψ y e_i = ∂_iΨ(y) and lineDeriv ℝ φ_i y (−e_i) = −∂_iφ_i(y). Hence ∫ ∂_iΨ·φ_i = −∫ Ψ·∂_iφ_i.
- On the open set B̆_{r+η/3}(0), where χ ≡ 1, we have φ_i = ∂_iG and ∂_iφ_i = D²G(·)(e_i, e_i). This set contains closedBall(0, r), outside of which Ψ and ∇Ψ vanish. Therefore ∫ ∂_iΨ·∂_iG = −∫ Ψ·D²G(·)(e_i, e_i).
- Summing over i: ∫ ⟨∇Ψ, ∇G⟩ = −∫ Ψ·ΔG = 0, because ΔG = 0 on V ⊇ closedBall(0, r).
- Finally ⟨∇Ψ(y), ∇G(y)⟩ = DG(y)(∇Ψ(y)) = −s·g(|y|²)·Dh(x − sy)(y). Hence s·∫ Dh(x − sy)(y)·g(|y|²) dy = 0, and since s > 0, M'(s) = 0.

5. (Proof of (i).) M is differentiable on I ⊇ [0, 1], so it is continuous on [0, 1] and differentiable on (0, 1). By the mean value theorem (exists_deriv_eq_slope / exists_hasDerivAt_eq_slope) there is c ∈ (0, 1) with M(1) − M(0) = M'(c), and M'(c) = 0 by step 4; so M(1) = M(0). (Also M'(0) = −Dh(x)(∫ y·g(|y|²) dy) = 0, because y ↦ y·g(|y|²) is odd. So M' = 0 on all of [0, 1], and constant_of_derivWithin_zero may be used instead.) We have M(0) = ∫ h(x)·g(|y|²) dy = h(x)·∫ g(|y|²) dy and M(1) = ∫ h(x − y)·g(|y|²) dy. This is (i).

6. (Proof of (ii).) For k ≥ 1 let g_k(t) := min{1, max{0, k(r² − t)}}.
- Each g_k is continuous, 0 ≤ g_k ≤ 1, and g_k(t) = 0 for t ≥ r².
- For every y, g_k(|y|²) → 1_{B̆_r(0)}(y). If |y| < r then g_k(|y|²) = 1 as soon as k(r² − |y|²) ≥ 1. If |y| ≥ r then g_k(|y|²) = 0 for all k.
- By (i), ∫ h(x − y)·g_k(|y|²) dy = h(x)·∫ g_k(|y|²) dy for every k.
- The two integrands are dominated by A₀·1_{closedBall(0,r)} and 1_{closedBall(0,r)}, both integrable. Dominated convergence gives ∫_{B̆_r(0)} h(x − y) dy = h(x)·Lⁿ(B̆_r(0)).
- The map y ↦ x − y preserves Lⁿ and maps B̆_r(0) onto B̆_r(x), and Lⁿ(B̆_r(0)) = Lⁿ(B̆_r(x)) < ∞. Hence ∫_{B̆_r(x)} h = h(x)·Lⁿ(B̆_r(x)) = (volume (ball x r)).toReal·h(x).
This is (ii). ∎

Part 2 (proof of the statement = Lemma IE; every reference to Lemma MV is to Part 1).
Lemma IE (interior estimates for harmonic functions; Simon 3.2–3.4). For every n ≥ 1 there is C_H > 0 such that the following holds for every R > 0 and every h : ℝⁿ → ℝ (ℝⁿ = Euclid n) satisfying: h is C^m on the open ball B := B̆_R(0) for every m ∈ ℕ; Δh(y) = Σ_i D²h(y)(e_i, e_i) = 0 for all y ∈ B (D²h(y)(a, b) = iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 h y ![a, b], e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1); ‖Dh‖² is integrable on B with ∫_B ‖Dh‖² ≤ Rⁿ; and h² is integrable on B (Dh = fderiv ℝ h, ‖·‖ the operator norm). Then (a) |h(0)| ≤ C_H·√((∫_B h²)/Rⁿ); (b) ‖Dh(0)‖ ≤ C_H; (c) |h(v) − h(0) − Dh(0)v| ≤ C_H‖v‖²/R for every v ∈ ℝⁿ with ‖v‖ ≤ R/4.
Proof of Lemma IE.
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 5, estimates 3.2–3.4 ("standard estimates for harmonic functions (which follow directly from the mean-value property)"). Here they are derived from the ball mean value property, Lemma MV(ii). The divergence-theorem step usually used for the derivative bound is replaced by comparing ball means over shifted balls.

Notation.
- B := B̆_R(0) (open), ω := Lⁿ(B̆_1(0)) ∈ (0, ∞), and Lⁿ(B̆_ρ(y)) = ωρⁿ (Measure.addHaar_ball, finrank ℝ (Euclid n) = n).
- ‖Dh(y)‖ = ‖fderiv ℝ h y‖ is the operator norm, equal to the Euclidean length of the gradient. D²h(y)(a, b) := iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 h y ![a, b] = D(Dh)(y)(a)(b).
- K₁ := 2ⁿω^{−1/2} and C_H := 4n·K₁ = 4n·2ⁿω^{−1/2} > 0; C_H depends only on n, and 2^{n/2}ω^{−1/2} ≤ K₁ ≤ C_H.
Fix R > 0 and h satisfying the hypotheses.

1. (Directional derivatives are harmonic.) Fix e ∈ ℝⁿ and let u_e(y) := Dh(y)e. Since h is C^m on B for every m, u_e is C^∞ on B, in particular C².
- For y ∈ B, the third derivative D³h(y) is symmetric in its three arguments. Symmetry of second derivatives (ContDiffAt.isSymmSndFDerivAt), applied to the C² maps h and Dh, gives symmetry in the last two slots and in the first two slots.
- Hence D²u_e(y)(a, b) = D³h(y)(a, b, e), and Δu_e(y) = Σ_i D³h(y)(e_i, e_i, e) = Σ_i D³h(y)(e, e_i, e_i) = D(Δh)(y)e.
- The right side is the derivative in direction e of z ↦ Δh(z) = Σ_i D²h(z)(e_i, e_i), which vanishes identically on the open set B. So Δu_e = 0 on B.
Thus h and every u_e are C² on the open set U := B with zero Laplacian, and Lemma MV(ii) applies to them on every closed ball contained in B.

2. (Mean value bounds.) Let y ∈ ℝⁿ and ρ > 0 with closedBall(y, ρ) ⊆ B.
(2a) h(y) = (ωρⁿ)^{−1}∫_{B̆_ρ(y)} h. By Cauchy–Schwarz, |h(y)| ≤ (ωρⁿ)^{−1}(ωρⁿ)^{1/2}(∫_{B̆_ρ(y)} h²)^{1/2} = (ωρⁿ)^{−1/2}(∫_{B̆_ρ(y)} h²)^{1/2}.
(2b) For a unit vector e, Dh(y)e = u_e(y) = (ωρⁿ)^{−1}∫_{B̆_ρ(y)} Dh(z)e dz ≤ (ωρⁿ)^{−1}∫_{B̆_ρ(y)} ‖Dh‖ ≤ (ωρⁿ)^{−1/2}(∫_{B̆_ρ(y)} ‖Dh‖²)^{1/2}. Replacing e by −e and taking the supremum over unit e gives ‖Dh(y)‖ ≤ (ωρⁿ)^{−1/2}(∫_B ‖Dh‖²)^{1/2} ≤ (ωρⁿ)^{−1/2}R^{n/2}.
The integrands are continuous on the compact set closedBall(y, ρ) ⊆ B. Since h² and ‖Dh‖² are integrable and nonnegative on B, their integrals over B̆_ρ(y) are at most those over B.

3. (Proof of (a) and (b).) closedBall(0, R/2) ⊆ B.
- (2a) with y = 0, ρ = R/2: |h(0)| ≤ (ω(R/2)ⁿ)^{−1/2}(∫_B h²)^{1/2} = 2^{n/2}ω^{−1/2}√((∫_B h²)/Rⁿ) ≤ C_H√((∫_B h²)/Rⁿ). This is (a).
- (2b) with y = 0, ρ = R/2: ‖Dh(0)‖ ≤ 2^{n/2}ω^{−1/2} ≤ C_H. This is (b).

4. (Gradient bound on closedBall(0, 5R/8).) If |y| ≤ 5R/8 then closedBall(y, R/4) ⊆ closedBall(0, 7R/8) ⊆ B. So (2b) with ρ = R/4 gives ‖Dh(y)‖ ≤ (ω(R/4)ⁿ)^{−1/2}R^{n/2} = 2ⁿω^{−1/2} = K₁.

5. (Second derivative bound on closedBall(0, R/4).) Let |x| ≤ R/4, let a and e be unit vectors, put ρ := R/4 and u := u_e, and let t ∈ ℝ with 0 < |t| ≤ R/8.
- closedBall(x, ρ) and closedBall(x + ta, ρ) lie in closedBall(0, 5R/8) ⊆ B. By the mean value property for u:
  u(x + ta) − u(x) = (ωρⁿ)^{−1}(∫_{B̆_ρ(x+ta)} u − ∫_{B̆_ρ(x)} u) = (ωρⁿ)^{−1}(∫_{S₁} u − ∫_{S₂} u),
  with S₁ := B̆_ρ(x+ta) ∖ B̆_ρ(x) and S₂ := B̆_ρ(x) ∖ B̆_ρ(x+ta).
- S₁ and S₂ are disjoint and contained in the annulus A_t := B̆_{ρ+|t|}(x) ∖ B̆_{ρ−|t|}(x). For z ∈ S₁: |z − x| ≥ ρ and |z − x| ≤ |z − x − ta| + |t| < ρ + |t|. For z ∈ S₂: |z − x| < ρ and |z − x| ≥ |z − x − ta| − |t| ≥ ρ − |t|.
- A_t ⊆ closedBall(0, 5R/8), where |u| ≤ ‖Dh‖ ≤ K₁ by step 4. Hence
  |u(x + ta) − u(x)| ≤ (ωρⁿ)^{−1}K₁·Lⁿ(A_t) = (ωρⁿ)^{−1}K₁ω((ρ + |t|)ⁿ − (ρ − |t|)ⁿ) ≤ K₁ρ^{−n}·2|t|·n(ρ + |t|)^{n−1},
  by the mean value theorem for τ ↦ τⁿ.
- Divide by |t| and let t → 0 (u is differentiable at x): |Du(x)a| ≤ 2nK₁/ρ = 8nK₁/R.
- Since Du(x)a = D(Dh)(x)(a)(e) = D²h(x)(a, e), we get |D²h(x)(a, e)| ≤ 8nK₁/R for all unit a, e. By bilinearity, |D²h(x)(v, v)| ≤ (8nK₁/R)|v|² for every v ∈ ℝⁿ whenever |x| ≤ R/4.

6. (Taylor expansion; proof of (c).) Let |v| ≤ R/4 and φ(τ) := h(τv) on the open interval J := {τ : |τ|·|v| < R} ⊇ [0, 1], on which τv ∈ B.
- φ is C² with φ'(τ) = Dh(τv)v and φ''(τ) = D²h(τv)(v, v).
- For τ ∈ [0, 1], |τv| ≤ R/4, so step 5 gives |φ''(τ)| ≤ S := 8nK₁|v|²/R.
- Let ψ(τ) := φ(τ) − φ(0) − τφ'(0). Then ψ(0) = 0 and, for τ ∈ [0, 1], |ψ'(τ)| = |φ'(τ) − φ'(0)| ≤ τS (mean value inequality for φ').
- Hence |ψ(1)| ≤ ∫_0^1 τS dτ = S/2 = 4nK₁|v|²/R = C_H|v|²/R.
Since ψ(1) = h(v) − h(0) − Dh(0)v, this is (c). ∎
proof_key_steps: Part 1 (Lemma MV). Let h be C² on an open U with zero Laplacian, with closedBall(x, r) ⊆ U. Differentiation under the integral sign shows that M(s) := ∫ h(x − sy)g(|y|²) dy is differentiable on an interval containing [0, 1]. Integration by parts against the compactly supported radial potential Ψ(y) = P(|y|²), with ∇Ψ(y) = g(|y|²)y, gives M' = 0 on (0, 1]. This is the radial-kernel identity (i). Dominated convergence with g_k → 1_{[0,r²)} then gives the ball identity (ii).
The directional derivatives u_e = Dh(·)e are C^∞ with zero Laplacian on B, by symmetry of D³h. So Lemma MV(ii) applies to h and to every u_e on closed balls contained in B.
Cauchy–Schwarz on ball means gives |h(y)| ≤ (ωρⁿ)^{−1/2}(∫ h²)^{1/2} and ‖Dh(y)‖ ≤ (ωρⁿ)^{−1/2}R^{n/2} whenever closedBall(y, ρ) ⊆ B. Taking y = 0 and ρ = R/2 gives (a) and (b).

On closedBall(0, 5R/8), ‖Dh‖ ≤ K₁ = 2ⁿω^{−1/2}. Compare the ball means of u_e over B̆_{R/4}(x + ta) and B̆_{R/4}(x); their difference is controlled by an annulus of measure ω((ρ + |t|)ⁿ − (ρ − |t|)ⁿ). This gives |D²h(x)(v, v)| ≤ (8nK₁/R)|v|² for |x| ≤ R/4.
The second-order Taylor expansion of τ ↦ h(τv), for ‖v‖ ≤ R/4, gives (c) with C_H = 4n·2ⁿω^{−1/2}, a constant depending only on n.

subproblems.statement: For every n ≥ 1 and every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with the following property. Let R₀ > 0 and let w : ℝⁿ → ℝ (ℝⁿ = Euclid n) be Lipschitz (with some constant Lw) with ∫_{B̆_{R₀}(0)} ‖Dw‖² ≤ R₀ⁿ. Provenance and scope. This is Lemma HA of the parent-supplied proof (Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 5, Lemma 3.1, the Harmonic Approximation Lemma, with its printed proof adapted to Lipschitz functions), made self-contained by proving in full, as Parts 1–5, every analytic input it uses: the mean value property (Lemma MV, used only in the proof of Lemma WL), Weyl's lemma (Lemma WL), the Poincaré inequality on the unit ball (Lemma PI), Rellich's compactness theorem (Lemma RC) and lower semicontinuity of the Dirichlet energy (Lemma EL). The statement and its frozen Lean type are character-identical to the comparator-accepted DAG node root.density_one_implies_regular-a1.epsilon_regularity-a1.allard_graph-a1.harmonic_approximation-a1.harmonic_approx-a1 (Submission.dorag_ha_approximation, candidate ddd06d0b6e7e9d371d11f9507e610d81aa4f2896). Apart from this preamble and the Part headings, the text below reproduces the parent's Lemmas MV, WL, PI, RC, EL and HA verbatim. It uses only theorems of the pinned Mathlib, cited by name, and no DAG declaration.

Global conventions.
- n ≥ 1 and ℝⁿ = Euclid n, with Euclidean norm |·| = ‖·‖ and inner product ⟨·,·⟩; Lⁿ := volume.
- B̆_ρ(y) is the open ball (Lean ball y ρ) and closedBall(y, ρ) the closed ball; B_ρ := B̆_ρ(0) unless a lemma fixes another meaning.
- e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1.
- For f differentiable at z: Df(z) := fderiv ℝ f z, whose operator norm ‖Df(z)‖ is the Euclidean length of the gradient ∇f(z), and ∂_if := Df(·)e_i.
- For f of class C² on an open set V and z ∈ V: D²f(z)(a, b) := iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 f z ![a, b] = D(Df)(z)(a)(b) (iteratedFDeriv_two_apply), and Δf(z) := Σ_i D²f(z)(e_i, e_i).
- "h is harmonic on V" means that h is C^m on V for every m ∈ ℕ and Δh = 0 on V.
- For Lipschitz u and C¹ ζ: ∇u·∇ζ := Σ_i Du(e_i)Dζ(e_i). This is exactly the Lean integrand Σ_i fderiv ℝ u v (e_i) * fderiv ℝ ζ v (e_i).
Each lemma below may fix further local notation, valid only inside that lemma.

Part 1 (Lemma MV, the mean value property; used in Part 2).
Lemma MV (mean value property). Let n ≥ 1, let U ⊆ ℝⁿ (= Euclid n) be open, and let h : ℝⁿ → ℝ be of class C² on U with Δh(y) := Σ_{i<n} D²h(y)(e_i, e_i) = 0 for every y ∈ U, where D²h(y)(a, b) = iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 h y ![a, b] and e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1. Let x ∈ ℝⁿ and r > 0 with closedBall(x, r) ⊆ U. Then (i) for every continuous g : ℝ → ℝ with g(t) = 0 for all t ≥ r², ∫_{ℝⁿ} h(x − y)·g(|y|²) dy = h(x)·∫_{ℝⁿ} g(|y|²) dy; and (ii) ∫_{B̆_r(x)} h = Lⁿ(B̆_r(x))·h(x), where Lⁿ = volume is Lebesgue measure, B̆_r(x) is the open ball and the measure is taken as a real number (ENNReal.toReal).
Proof of Lemma MV.
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 5, 3.2–3.4 calls these "standard estimates for harmonic functions (which follow directly from the mean-value property)"; cf. Evans, PDE, §2.2.2, and Gilbarg–Trudinger, Thm 2.1. The proof below uses neither surface measure nor the divergence theorem. It needs only differentiation under the integral sign and integration by parts for compactly supported C¹ (hence Lipschitz) functions. Mathlib's only mean value theorem for harmonic functions is for ℂ (Analysis/Complex/Harmonic/MeanValue.lean), so a general-n proof is required.

Conventions.
- |·| and ⟨·,·⟩ are the Euclidean norm and inner product on ℝⁿ = Euclid n, and Lⁿ = volume.
- For f differentiable at z: Df(z) = fderiv ℝ f z; ∇f(z) is the vector with Df(z)v = ⟨∇f(z), v⟩; ∂_if := Df(·)e_i.
- If f is C² on an open set V and z ∈ V, then iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 f z ![a, b] = D(Df)(z)(a)(b) =: D²f(z)(a, b) (iteratedFDeriv_two_apply), and Δf(z) := Σ_i D²f(z)(e_i, e_i). Since V is open, these are the classical derivatives.

1. (Room around the ball.) closedBall(x, r) is compact and lies in the open set U. So there is η > 0 with closedBall(x, r + η) ⊆ U (IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open and cthickening_closedBall). Put r' := r + η. Since h is C² on U, h and Dh are continuous on the compact set closedBall(x, r'). Let A₀ := sup|h| and A₁ := sup‖Dh‖ over closedBall(x, r'); both are finite.

2. (A radial potential.) Fix a continuous g : ℝ → ℝ with g(t) = 0 for t ≥ r², and let γ := sup_{0 ≤ t ≤ r²}|g(t)|.
- Put P(t) := ½∫_{r²}^{t} g(τ) dτ. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, P is C¹ with P' = g/2. Also P(t) = 0 for t ≥ r², since g vanishes on [r², t].
- Put Ψ(y) := P(|y|²). Then Ψ is C¹ on ℝⁿ with DΨ(y)v = 2P'(|y|²)⟨y, v⟩, i.e. ∇Ψ(y) = g(|y|²)·y.
- If |y| ≥ r then Ψ(y) = 0 and ∇Ψ(y) = 0. So Ψ is C¹ with compact support in closedBall(0, r), and in particular Lipschitz (ContDiff.lipschitzWith_of_hasCompactSupport).

3. (The function M and its derivative.) Let κ := r'/r > 1 and I := (1 − κ, κ), an open interval containing [0, 1]. For s ∈ I and |y| ≤ r we have |sy| < κr = r', so x − sy ∈ closedBall(x, r') ⊆ U. Define F(s, y) := h(x − sy)·g(|y|²) and M(s) := ∫_{ℝⁿ} F(s, y) dy for s ∈ I.
- If |y| ≥ r then g(|y|²) = 0, so F(s, y) = 0 whatever h(x − sy) is. Thus F(s, ·) is the extension by zero of a function continuous on closedBall(0, r). It is measurable, satisfies |F(s, y)| ≤ A₀γ·1_{closedBall(0,r)}(y), and is integrable.
- For |y| ≤ r, s ↦ F(s, y) is differentiable on I with derivative −Dh(x − sy)(y)·g(|y|²), by the chain rule (h is differentiable on U). For |y| ≥ r it is identically 0, with derivative 0.
- In every case the derivative is bounded by A₁rγ·1_{closedBall(0,r)}(y), which is integrable and independent of s.
By differentiation under the integral sign (hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le), M is differentiable on I with M'(s) = −∫ Dh(x − sy)(y)·g(|y|²) dy, the integrand being 0 for |y| ≥ r. In particular M is continuous on [0, 1].

4. (M' = 0 on (0, 1].) Fix s ∈ (0, 1] and let G(y) := h(x − sy).
- For y in the open ball V := B̆_{r'}(0) we have |sy| < r', so x − sy ∈ closedBall(x, r') ⊆ U. Hence G is C² on V with DG(y) = −s·Dh(x − sy) and D²G(y)(a, b) = s²·D²h(x − sy)(a, b). So ΔG(y) = s²·Δh(x − sy) = 0 for y ∈ V.
- Choose χ ∈ C^∞(ℝⁿ) with χ ≡ 1 on B̆_{r+η/3}(0) and tsupport χ = closedBall(0, r + 2η/3) ⊆ V: a ContDiffBump centred at 0 with rIn = r + η/3 and rOut = r + 2η/3 (ContDiffBump.tsupport_eq). B̆_{r+η/3}(0) is an open neighbourhood of closedBall(0, r).
- For each i let φ_i := χ·∂_iG on V and φ_i := 0 off V. Then φ_i is C¹ on ℝⁿ: ∂_iG is C¹ on V, φ_i vanishes on the open set ℝⁿ ∖ tsupport χ, and these two open sets cover ℝⁿ. φ_i has compact support, hence is Lipschitz.
- By LipschitzWith.integral_lineDeriv_mul_eq with f := Ψ, g := φ_i, v := e_i:
  ∫ lineDeriv ℝ Ψ y e_i · φ_i(y) dy = ∫ lineDeriv ℝ φ_i y (−e_i) · Ψ(y) dy.
  Both functions are differentiable everywhere, so lineDeriv ℝ Ψ y e_i = ∂_iΨ(y) and lineDeriv ℝ φ_i y (−e_i) = −∂_iφ_i(y). Hence ∫ ∂_iΨ·φ_i = −∫ Ψ·∂_iφ_i.
- On the open set B̆_{r+η/3}(0), where χ ≡ 1, we have φ_i = ∂_iG and ∂_iφ_i = D²G(·)(e_i, e_i). This set contains closedBall(0, r), outside of which Ψ and ∇Ψ vanish. Therefore ∫ ∂_iΨ·∂_iG = −∫ Ψ·D²G(·)(e_i, e_i).
- Summing over i: ∫ ⟨∇Ψ, ∇G⟩ = −∫ Ψ·ΔG = 0, because ΔG = 0 on V ⊇ closedBall(0, r).
- Finally ⟨∇Ψ(y), ∇G(y)⟩ = DG(y)(∇Ψ(y)) = −s·g(|y|²)·Dh(x − sy)(y). Hence s·∫ Dh(x − sy)(y)·g(|y|²) dy = 0, and since s > 0, M'(s) = 0.

5. (Proof of (i).) M is differentiable on I ⊇ [0, 1], so it is continuous on [0, 1] and differentiable on (0, 1). By the mean value theorem (exists_deriv_eq_slope / exists_hasDerivAt_eq_slope) there is c ∈ (0, 1) with M(1) − M(0) = M'(c), and M'(c) = 0 by step 4; so M(1) = M(0). (Also M'(0) = −Dh(x)(∫ y·g(|y|²) dy) = 0, because y ↦ y·g(|y|²) is odd. So M' = 0 on all of [0, 1], and constant_of_derivWithin_zero may be used instead.) We have M(0) = ∫ h(x)·g(|y|²) dy = h(x)·∫ g(|y|²) dy and M(1) = ∫ h(x − y)·g(|y|²) dy. This is (i).

6. (Proof of (ii).) For k ≥ 1 let g_k(t) := min{1, max{0, k(r² − t)}}.
- Each g_k is continuous, 0 ≤ g_k ≤ 1, and g_k(t) = 0 for t ≥ r².
- For every y, g_k(|y|²) → 1_{B̆_r(0)}(y). If |y| < r then g_k(|y|²) = 1 as soon as k(r² − |y|²) ≥ 1. If |y| ≥ r then g_k(|y|²) = 0 for all k.
- By (i), ∫ h(x − y)·g_k(|y|²) dy = h(x)·∫ g_k(|y|²) dy for every k.
- The two integrands are dominated by A₀·1_{closedBall(0,r)} and 1_{closedBall(0,r)}, both integrable. Dominated convergence gives ∫_{B̆_r(0)} h(x − y) dy = h(x)·Lⁿ(B̆_r(0)).
- The map y ↦ x − y preserves Lⁿ and maps B̆_r(0) onto B̆_r(x), and Lⁿ(B̆_r(0)) = Lⁿ(B̆_r(x)) < ∞. Hence ∫_{B̆_r(x)} h = h(x)·Lⁿ(B̆_r(x)) = (volume (ball x r)).toReal·h(x).
This is (ii). ∎

Part 2 (Lemma WL, Weyl's lemma; every reference to Lemma MV is to Part 1).
Lemma WL (Weyl's lemma). Let n ≥ 1, R > 0, and let W : ℝⁿ → ℝ (ℝⁿ = Euclid n) be integrable on B := B̆_R(0). Suppose ∫_B W·Δζ = 0 for every ζ : ℝⁿ → ℝ of class C² with compact support and tsupport ζ ⊆ B, where Δζ(y) = Σ_i iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 ζ y ![e_i, e_i] and e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1. Then there is h : ℝⁿ → ℝ which is C^m on B for every m ∈ ℕ, satisfies Σ_i iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 h y ![e_i, e_i] = 0 at every y ∈ B, and agrees with W Lⁿ-almost everywhere on B.
Proof of Lemma WL.
Source: Weyl's lemma, implicit in Simon's proof of Lemma 5.3.1 ("Thus w is harmonic in B"). The proof is by mollification with a radial kernel (cf. Evans, PDE, §2.2.3, Thm 6 and its proof). The mean value property used is Lemma MV(i).

0. (Radial mollifier.) Let B := B̆_R(0), ω := Lⁿ(B̆_1(0)), and W̃ := 1_B·W ∈ L¹(ℝⁿ).
- Let θ := Real.smoothTransition. It is C^∞, θ = 0 on (−∞, 0], θ > 0 on (0, ∞), and 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1.
- Put ρ₀(y) := θ(1 − |y|²). ρ₀ is C^∞ (a composition of C^∞ maps, since |y|² = ⟨y, y⟩). Also ρ₀ ≥ 0, ρ₀(y) > 0 iff |y| < 1, and tsupport ρ₀ = closedBall(0, 1).
- c₀ := ∫ρ₀ ∈ (0, ∞), and ρ := ρ₀/c₀, so ∫ρ = 1.
- For ε > 0 put ρ_ε(y) := ε^{−n}ρ(y/ε). Then ρ_ε(y) = ĝ_ε(|y|²) with ĝ_ε(t) := ε^{−n}c₀^{−1}θ(1 − t/ε²); ĝ_ε is continuous and vanishes for t ≥ ε².
- ρ_ε is C^∞, ρ_ε ≥ 0, ρ_ε vanishes off B̆_ε(0), ∫ρ_ε = 1 (linear change of variables), and sup ρ_ε = ε^{−n} sup ρ.

1. (Mollification.) For ε > 0 let W_ε(x) := ∫ W̃(y)ρ_ε(x − y) dy = (ρ_ε ⋆ W̃)(x), Mathlib's convolution with lsmul.
- ρ_ε is C^∞ with compact support and W̃ is integrable, hence locally integrable. So W_ε is C^∞ on ℝⁿ (HasCompactSupport.contDiff_convolution_left).
- Its derivatives are convolutions with the derivatives of ρ_ε (HasCompactSupport.hasFDerivAt_convolution_left, applied twice). In particular D²W_ε(x)(a, b) = ∫ W̃(y)·D²ρ_ε(x − y)(a, b) dy, and ΔW_ε(x) = ∫ W̃(y)·(Δρ_ε)(x − y) dy.

2. (W_ε is harmonic on B̆_{R−ε}(0).) Let 0 < ε < R and |x| < R − ε. Put ζ_x(y) := ρ_ε(x − y).
- ζ_x is C^∞, hence C². It vanishes off B̆_ε(x), so it has compact support and tsupport ζ_x ⊆ closedBall(x, ε) ⊆ B (as |x| + ε < R).
- By the chain rule, D²ζ_x(y)(a, b) = D²ρ_ε(x − y)(−a, −b) = D²ρ_ε(x − y)(a, b). Hence Δζ_x(y) = (Δρ_ε)(x − y).
- Therefore ΔW_ε(x) = ∫ W̃·Δζ_x = ∫_B W·Δζ_x = 0 by the hypothesis, since W̃ = W on B and W̃ = 0 off B.
So W_ε is C² on the open ball B̆_{R−ε}(0) and its Laplacian vanishes there.

3. (Mean value property.) Let ε, δ > 0 and |x| + ε + δ < R. Apply Lemma MV(i) with U := B̆_{R−ε}(0), h := W_ε, the point x, r := δ and g := ĝ_δ. The hypothesis closedBall(x, δ) ⊆ U holds because |x| + δ < R − ε. This gives ∫ W_ε(x − z)ρ_δ(z) dz = W_ε(x)·∫ρ_δ = W_ε(x).

4. (Symmetry in ε, δ.) With x, ε, δ as in step 3:
∫ W_ε(x − z)ρ_δ(z) dz = ∫∫ W̃(y)ρ_ε(x − z − y)ρ_δ(z) dy dz = ∫ W̃(y)(∫ ρ_ε(x − y − z)ρ_δ(z) dz) dy.
- Fubini applies, because the absolute integrand has integral at most sup ρ_ε·‖W̃‖_{L¹}·∫ρ_δ < ∞.
- The inner integral is (ρ_ε ⋆ ρ_δ)(x − y), and ρ_ε ⋆ ρ_δ = ρ_δ ⋆ ρ_ε (substitute z ↦ (x − y) − z). So the left side is symmetric in (ε, δ).
- Step 3 for (ε, δ) and for (δ, ε) has the same hypothesis. Hence W_ε(x) = W_δ(x) whenever ε, δ > 0 and |x| + ε + δ < R.

5. (Definition and regularity of h.) For x ∈ B put h(x) := W_{(R−|x|)/3}(x); for x ∉ B put h(x) := 0.
- Claim: if 0 < r < R and 0 < ε ≤ (R − r)/3, then h = W_ε on B̆_r(0). Indeed, for |x| < r, ε + (R − |x|)/3 + |x| ≤ 2(R − |x|)/3 + |x| < R. So step 4 gives W_ε(x) = W_{(R−|x|)/3}(x) = h(x).
- Consequently, on each open ball B̆_r(0) with r < R, h coincides with the C^∞ function W_{(R−r)/3}. By step 2 that function has zero Laplacian on B̆_{(2R+r)/3}(0) ⊇ B̆_r(0).
- Functions that agree on an open set have the same iterated derivatives there (Filter.EventuallyEq.iteratedFDeriv). So h is C^m on B̆_r(0) for every m, and Σ_i iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 h y ![e_i, e_i] = 0 for y ∈ B̆_r(0).
- B = ⋃_{r<R} B̆_r(0), and C^m regularity on an open set is a local property. Hence h is C^m on B for every m ∈ ℕ and its Laplacian vanishes on B.

6. (h = W a.e. on B.)
- By the Lebesgue differentiation theorem for W̃ ∈ L¹(ℝⁿ), for Lⁿ-a.e. x we have ⨍_{closedBall(x,ε)} |W̃(y) − W̃(x)| dy → 0 as ε → 0+ (VitaliFamily.ae_tendsto_average_norm_sub for the Besicovitch Vitali family, or IsUnifLocDoublingMeasure.ae_tendsto_average_norm_sub; both use closed balls).
- At such x, since ∫ρ_ε = 1, ρ_ε(x − ·) vanishes off closedBall(x, ε), and Lⁿ(closedBall(x, ε)) = ωεⁿ (spheres are null):
  |W_ε(x) − W̃(x)| = |∫ (W̃(y) − W̃(x))ρ_ε(x − y) dy| ≤ ε^{−n}·sup ρ·∫_{closedBall(x,ε)} |W̃(y) − W̃(x)| dy = ω·sup ρ·⨍_{closedBall(x,ε)} |W̃ − W̃(x)| → 0.
  (tendsto_integral_smul_of_tendsto_average_norm_sub with a_ε := closedBall(x, ε) packages this estimate.)
- If moreover x ∈ B, step 5 with r := (R + |x|)/2 gives W_ε(x) = h(x) for all 0 < ε ≤ (R − |x|)/6. Hence h(x) = lim_{ε→0} W_ε(x) = W̃(x) = W(x).
Therefore h = W Lⁿ-a.e. on B, i.e. ∀ᵐ y ∂(volume.restrict B), h y = W y. ∎

Part 3 (Lemma PI, the Poincaré inequality on the unit ball).
Lemma PI (Poincaré inequality on the unit ball). For every n ≥ 1 there is C_P > 0 such that every Lipschitz u : ℝⁿ → ℝ (ℝⁿ = Euclid n) satisfies ∫_B (u − ū)² ≤ C_P·∫_B ‖Du‖². Here B := B̆_1(0) is the open unit ball, ū := (∫_B u)/Lⁿ(B) is the mean of u over B (Lⁿ = volume, taken as a real number), and Du = fderiv ℝ u with the operator norm.
Proof of Lemma PI.
Source: the Poincaré inequality on a ball cited in Simon's proof of Lemma 5.3.1 ("by the Poincaré inequality (see e.g. [GT01])"). This is the convex-domain argument of Gilbarg–Trudinger, Lemma 7.16 and (7.45), written out for Lipschitz functions. It gives C_P = 2^{n+2}.

0. (Setup.) B := B̆_1(0), ω := Lⁿ(B) ∈ (0, ∞), and ū := ω^{−1}∫_B u, which is the expression (∫_B u)/(volume B).toReal of the statement. Let L be a Lipschitz constant of u.
- u is continuous and bounded on B. Du = fderiv ℝ u is Borel measurable (measurable_fderiv) with ‖Du(z)‖ ≤ L for all z (norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz). So every integral below is a finite Lebesgue integral of a bounded measurable function over a bounded set.
- N := {z : u is not differentiable at z} is Borel (measurableSet_of_differentiableAt) and Lⁿ-null (Rademacher: LipschitzWith.ae_differentiableAt).

1. (FTC on segments.) Let x, y ∈ ℝⁿ satisfy L¹({t ∈ [0, 1] : (1 − t)y + tx ∈ N}) = 0. Then u(x) − u(y) = ∫_0^1 Du((1 − t)y + tx)(x − y) dt.
Proof: φ(t) := u((1 − t)y + tx) is Lipschitz on ℝ, hence absolutely continuous on [0, 1] (LipschitzOnWith.absolutelyContinuousOnInterval). So φ(1) − φ(0) = ∫_0^1 deriv φ (AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval.integral_deriv_eq_sub). For a.e. t ∈ [0, 1], u is differentiable at (1 − t)y + tx, and the chain rule then gives deriv φ(t) = Du((1 − t)y + tx)(x − y).

2. (Almost every pair.) Let E := {(x, y, t) ∈ ℝⁿ × ℝⁿ × [0, 1] : (1 − t)y + tx ∈ N}, a Borel set.
- For fixed y and t ∈ (0, 1], the x-section of E is t^{−1}(N − (1 − t)y), which is Lⁿ-null. By Tonelli (integrating first in x; the slice t = 0 is L¹-null), E is null.
- By Tonelli again (integrating first in t), for Lⁿ⊗Lⁿ-a.e. (x, y) the t-section of E is L¹-null, so step 1 applies.
Hence for a.e. (x, y): u(x) − u(y) = ∫_0^1 Du((1 − t)y + tx)(x − y) dt.

3. (Pointwise bound.) For a.e. (x, y) ∈ B × B we have |x − y| < 2, so Cauchy–Schwarz on [0, 1] gives
(u(x) − u(y))² ≤ |x − y|²(∫_0^1 ‖Du((1 − t)y + tx)‖ dt)² ≤ 4∫_0^1 ‖Du((1 − t)y + tx)‖² dt.

4. (Averaging.) For x ∈ B, u(x) − ū = ω^{−1}∫_B (u(x) − u(y)) dy. By Cauchy–Schwarz, (u(x) − ū)² ≤ ω^{−1}∫_B (u(x) − u(y))² dy. Integrate over x ∈ B and use step 3 and Tonelli:
∫_B (u − ū)² ≤ ω^{−1}∫_B∫_B (u(x) − u(y))² dy dx ≤ 4ω^{−1}∫_0^1 I(t) dt, where I(t) := ∫_B∫_B ‖Du((1 − t)y + tx)‖² dy dx.

5. (Change of variables.) B is convex, so (1 − t)y + tx ∈ B for x, y ∈ B and t ∈ [0, 1].
- If t ∈ [1/2, 1], fix y ∈ B. The affine bijection x ↦ (1 − t)y + tx has Jacobian tⁿ ≥ 2^{−n} and maps B into B. Hence ∫_B ‖Du((1 − t)y + tx)‖² dx = t^{−n}∫_{(1−t)y+tB} ‖Du‖² ≤ 2ⁿ∫_B ‖Du‖². (Use Measure.setIntegral_comp_smul_of_pos or Measure.map_addHaar_smul, together with translation invariance, for the nonnegative function 1_B‖Du‖².) Integrating over y ∈ B gives I(t) ≤ 2ⁿω∫_B ‖Du‖².
- If t ∈ [0, 1/2], fix x ∈ B and change variables in y instead; the Jacobian is (1 − t)ⁿ ≥ 2^{−n}. With Tonelli, again I(t) ≤ 2ⁿω∫_B ‖Du‖².

6. (Conclusion.) ∫_B (u − ū)² ≤ 4ω^{−1}·2ⁿω∫_B ‖Du‖² = 2^{n+2}∫_B ‖Du‖². So C_P := 2^{n+2} > 0 works, and it depends only on n. ∎

Part 4 (Lemma RC, Rellich's compactness theorem on the unit ball).
Lemma RC (Rellich's compactness theorem on the unit ball). Let n ≥ 1, M ∈ ℝ, and let (u_j)_{j∈ℕ} be Lipschitz functions ℝⁿ → ℝ (ℝⁿ = Euclid n, each u_j with its own Lipschitz constant) such that ∫_B u_j² ≤ M and ∫_B ‖Du_j‖² ≤ M for every j, where B := B̆_1(0) is the open unit ball and Du_j = fderiv ℝ u_j. Then there are a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ and W : ℝⁿ → ℝ with W ∈ L²(B) (MemLp W 2 for Lebesgue measure restricted to B) such that ∫_B (u_{φ(j)} − W)² → 0 as j → ∞.
Proof of Lemma RC.
Source: Rellich's compactness theorem, as used in Simon's proof of Lemma 5.3.1 ("by Rellich's theorem (see [GT01])"; Gilbarg–Trudinger Thm 7.22, Evans §5.7 Thm 1). W^{1,2} is not available, so it is proved here directly for Lipschitz functions. The proof combines interior mollification and Arzelà–Ascoli with a boundary-layer estimate obtained from rays and dilations.

0. (Notation and tools.) B := B̆_1(0), B_r := B̆_r(0), A_s := B ∖ B_{1−s}, K_s := closedBall(0, 1 − s), ω := Lⁿ(B).
- M ≥ 0 automatically, since the integrals are ≥ 0.
- For a Lipschitz u, its non-differentiability set N_u is Borel and Lⁿ-null (measurableSet_of_differentiableAt, LipschitzWith.ae_differentiableAt). Du is Borel and bounded (measurable_fderiv, norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz).
- One-variable FTC: a Lipschitz φ : ℝ → ℝ satisfies φ(b) − φ(a) = ∫_a^b deriv φ (LipschitzOnWith.absolutelyContinuousOnInterval and AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval.integral_deriv_eq_sub). If φ(τ) = u(p + τv) and u is differentiable at p + τv, then deriv φ(τ) = Du(p + τv)v.

1. (FTC along translations.) Let u be Lipschitz and z ∈ ℝⁿ. Then for a.e. p ∈ ℝⁿ, u(p + z) − u(p) = ∫_0^1 Du(p + τz)z dτ.
Proof: {(p, τ) ∈ ℝⁿ × [0, 1] : p + τz ∈ N_u} is Borel with null p-sections N_u − τz. By Tonelli, for a.e. p its τ-section is null, and the one-variable FTC applies to τ ↦ u(p + τz).

2. (Interior mollification.) Let ρ̂(z) := c₁(1 − |z|)₊ with c₁ := (∫(1 − |z|)₊ dz)^{−1}.
- ρ̂ ≥ 0, ρ̂ = 0 off B̆_1(0), ∫ρ̂ = 1, sup ρ̂ = c₁, and ρ̂ is c₁-Lipschitz.
- For ε > 0 put ρ̂_ε(w) := ε^{−n}ρ̂(w/ε). It vanishes off B̆_ε(0), has supremum ε^{−n}c₁ and Lipschitz constant ε^{−n−1}c₁.
- For a Lipschitz u let u_ε(x) := ∫ u(x − εz)ρ̂(z) dz = ∫ u(y)ρ̂_ε(x − y) dy.
(2a) If 0 < ε ≤ s ≤ 1/2 then ∫_{B_{1−s}} (u − u_ε)² ≤ ε²∫_B ‖Du‖².
- For x ∈ B_{1−s}, u(x) − u_ε(x) = ∫ (u(x) − u(x − εz))ρ̂(z) dz.
- By step 1 (vector εz, base point p = x − εz; translations preserve null sets) and Tonelli in (x, z), for a.e. x and a.e. z with |z| < 1:
  |u(x) − u(x − εz)| = |∫_0^1 Du(x − εz + τεz)(εz) dτ| ≤ ε∫_0^1 ‖Du(x − (1 − τ)εz)‖ dτ.
- ρ̂(z)dz ⊗ dτ is a probability measure on B̆_1(0) × [0, 1]. So by Jensen, for a.e. x ∈ B_{1−s}:
  (u(x) − u_ε(x))² ≤ ε²∫ρ̂(z)∫_0^1 ‖Du(x − (1 − τ)εz)‖² dτ dz.
- Integrate over x ∈ B_{1−s} and use Tonelli. For each (z, τ) the translation x ↦ x − (1 − τ)εz maps B_{1−s} into B, because |(1 − τ)εz| < ε ≤ s. So ∫_{B_{1−s}} ‖Du(x − (1 − τ)εz)‖² dx ≤ ∫_B ‖Du‖², and (2a) follows.
(2b) Let 0 < ε ≤ s/2 ≤ 1/4 and x, x' ∈ K_s. Then B̆_ε(x) ∪ B̆_ε(x') ⊆ B, since 1 − s + s/2 < 1, and
- |u_ε(x)| ≤ ε^{−n}c₁∫_B |u| ≤ ε^{−n}c₁(ω∫_B u²)^{1/2};
- |u_ε(x) − u_ε(x')| ≤ ε^{−n−1}c₁|x − x'|∫_B |u| ≤ ε^{−n−1}c₁(ω∫_B u²)^{1/2}|x − x'|.

3. (Boundary layer.) For 0 < s ≤ 1/2 and Lipschitz u: ∫_{A_s} u² ≤ 2^{n+3}s(∫_B u² + ∫_B ‖Du‖²).
(i) {(x, σ) ∈ ℝⁿ × [1/2, 1] : σx ∈ N_u} is Borel with null x-sections σ^{−1}N_u. So for a.e. x, u is differentiable at σx for a.e. σ ∈ [1/2, 1]. For such x and every t ∈ [1/2, 1], the one-variable FTC for σ ↦ u(σx) gives u(x) − u(tx) = ∫_t^1 Du(σx)x dσ.
(ii) For such x ∈ A_s (so |x| < 1): |u(x)| ≤ |u(tx)| + ∫_{1/2}^1 ‖Du(σx)‖ dσ. Hence, by Cauchy–Schwarz on an interval of length 1/2,
u(x)² ≤ 2u(tx)² + 2(∫_{1/2}^1 ‖Du(σx)‖ dσ)² ≤ 2u(tx)² + ∫_{1/2}^1 ‖Du(σx)‖² dσ.
Averaging over t ∈ [1/2, 1]: u(x)² ≤ 4∫_{1/2}^1 u(tx)² dt + ∫_{1/2}^1 ‖Du(σx)‖² dσ.
(iii) Integrate over x ∈ A_s (Tonelli): ∫_{A_s} u² ≤ 4∫_{1/2}^1∫_{A_s} u(tx)² dx dt + ∫_{1/2}^1∫_{A_s} ‖Du(σx)‖² dx dσ.
(iv) Let F ≥ 0 be measurable and t ∈ [1/2, 1]. Then ∫_{A_s} F(tx) dx = t^{−n}∫_{tA_s} F ≤ 2ⁿ∫_B F·1_{tA_s}, where tA_s = {y : t(1 − s) ≤ |y| < t} ⊆ B.
By Tonelli, ∫_{1/2}^1∫_{A_s} F(tx) dx dt ≤ 2ⁿ∫_B F(y)ℓ(y) dy, where ℓ(y) := L¹{t ∈ [1/2, 1] : |y| < t ≤ |y|/(1 − s)} ≤ |y|s/(1 − s) ≤ 2s.
Hence ∫_{1/2}^1∫_{A_s} F(tx) dx dt ≤ 2^{n+1}s∫_B F.
(v) Apply (iv) with F = u² and with F = ‖Du‖²: ∫_{A_s} u² ≤ 4·2^{n+1}s∫_B u² + 2^{n+1}s∫_B ‖Du‖² ≤ 2^{n+3}s(∫_B u² + ∫_B ‖Du‖²).

4. (Total boundedness.) Let 𝓛 := Lp ℝ 2 (volume.restrict B), a complete metric space. Let f_j ∈ 𝓛 be the class of u_j; it is in L² because u_j is continuous and bounded on B. Fix η > 0.
- Choose s ∈ (0, 1/2] with 2^{n+3}s·2M ≤ η²/16, and ε ∈ (0, s/2] with ε²M ≤ η²/16.
- By step 3, ‖u_j‖_{L²(A_s)} ≤ η/4 for all j. By (2a), ‖u_j − (u_j)_ε‖_{L²(B_{1−s})} ≤ η/4 for all j.
- By (2b), the restrictions v_j := (u_j)_ε|_{K_s} to the compact set K_s are uniformly bounded and uniformly Lipschitz, hence equicontinuous. By the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem (BoundedContinuousFunction.arzela_ascoli on the compact space K_s), {v_j} is relatively compact, hence totally bounded, for the sup distance.
- So there are indices j_1, …, j_m such that every j has some k with sup_{K_s}|v_j − v_{j_k}| ≤ η/(4√ω).
- Since B = B_{1−s} ∪ A_s and B_{1−s} ⊆ K_s:
  ‖f_j − f_{j_k}‖_𝓛 ≤ ‖u_j‖_{L²(A_s)} + ‖u_{j_k}‖_{L²(A_s)} + ‖u_j − v_j‖_{L²(B_{1−s})} + √ω·sup_{K_s}|v_j − v_{j_k}| + ‖v_{j_k} − u_{j_k}‖_{L²(B_{1−s})} ≤ 5η/4.
η > 0 was arbitrary, so {f_j : j ∈ ℕ} is totally bounded in 𝓛.

5. (Extraction.) In the complete space 𝓛, the closure of a totally bounded set is totally bounded and closed, hence compact (TotallyBounded.closure, TotallyBounded.isCompact_of_isClosed). By IsCompact.tendsto_subseq there are a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ and F ∈ 𝓛 with f_{φ(j)} → F in 𝓛. Let W : ℝⁿ → ℝ be a representative of F, so MemLp W 2 (volume.restrict B). Then ∫_B (u_{φ(j)} − W)² = ‖f_{φ(j)} − F‖²_𝓛 → 0. ∎

Part 5 (Lemma EL, lower semicontinuity of the Dirichlet energy).
Lemma EL (lower semicontinuity of the Dirichlet energy). Let n ≥ 1, R > 0, B := B̆_R(0) ⊆ ℝⁿ (ℝⁿ = Euclid n), and E ∈ ℝ. Let (u_j)_{j∈ℕ} be Lipschitz functions ℝⁿ → ℝ with ∫_B ‖Du_j‖² ≤ E for all j, (c_j)_{j∈ℕ} real numbers, W : ℝⁿ → ℝ with W ∈ L²(B) and ∫_B (u_j − c_j − W)² → 0, and h : ℝⁿ → ℝ of class C² on B with h = W Lⁿ-almost everywhere on B (D = fderiv ℝ, operator norm). Then ‖Dh‖² is integrable on B and ∫_B ‖Dh‖² ≤ E.
Proof of Lemma EL.
Source: in the Lipschitz/L² setting of the frozen statements, this replaces one step of Simon's proof of Lemma 5.3.1: "∇f_{k'} ⇀ ∇w weakly in L², with ∫_B|∇w|² ≤ 1" (weak lower semicontinuity of the Dirichlet energy). The proof is by duality against compactly supported C¹ vector fields.

Notation.
- B := B̆_R(0), and e_i is the standard basis.
- For a vector field Φ = (Φ_1, …, Φ_n): divΦ := Σ_i ∂_iΦ_i and |Φ|² := Σ_i Φ_i².
- For u differentiable at y: ∇u·Φ(y) := Σ_i Du(y)(e_i)Φ_i(y). By Cauchy–Schwarz, |∇u·Φ| ≤ ‖Du(y)‖·|Φ(y)|, since the operator norm ‖Du(y)‖ is the Euclidean length of the gradient.
- 𝒱 is the set of Φ whose components are C¹ on ℝⁿ with compact support and tsupport Φ_i ⊆ B.

0. E ≥ 0, because E ≥ ∫_B ‖Du_0‖² ≥ 0.

1. (IBP for Lipschitz functions.) If u is Lipschitz and Φ ∈ 𝒱, then ∫_B ∇u·Φ = −∫_B u·divΦ and ∫_B divΦ = 0.
Proof: each Φ_i is C¹ with compact support, hence Lipschitz (ContDiff.lipschitzWith_of_hasCompactSupport). LipschitzWith.integral_lineDeriv_mul_eq with f := u, g := Φ_i, v := e_i gives
∫ lineDeriv ℝ u y e_i·Φ_i(y) dy = ∫ lineDeriv ℝ Φ_i y (−e_i)·u(y) dy = −∫ ∂_iΦ_i(y)·u(y) dy.
By Rademacher (LipschitzWith.ae_differentiableAt), for a.e. y, u is differentiable at y and lineDeriv ℝ u y e_i = Du(y)e_i. Sum over i. All integrands vanish outside ⋃_i tsupport Φ_i ⊆ B, so the integrals over ℝⁿ equal those over B. Taking u ≡ 1 (Du = 0) gives ∫_B divΦ = 0.

2. (IBP for h.) If Φ ∈ 𝒱 then ∫_B ∇h·Φ = −∫_B h·divΦ.
Proof:
- K := ⋃_i tsupport Φ_i is a compact subset of B, so K ⊆ closedBall(0, r₁) for some r₁ < R.
- Choose χ ∈ C^∞(ℝⁿ) with χ ≡ 1 on B̆_{r₂}(0) and tsupport χ ⊆ closedBall(0, r₃), where r₁ < r₂ < r₃ < R (a ContDiffBump).
- Put h̃ := χh on B and h̃ := 0 off B. Then h̃ is C² on ℝⁿ (C² on B, and zero on the open set ℝⁿ ∖ tsupport χ), has compact support, is Lipschitz, and is differentiable everywhere.
- The computation of step 1 with u := h̃ gives ∫ ∇h̃·Φ = −∫ h̃·divΦ. On the open set B̆_{r₂}(0) ⊇ K we have h̃ = h and Dh̃ = Dh, and both integrands vanish off K.

3. (Duality bound.) For Φ ∈ 𝒱: ∫_B ∇h·Φ ≤ √E·(∫_B |Φ|²)^{1/2}.
Proof:
- By step 2 and h = W a.e. on B, ∫_B ∇h·Φ = −∫_B W·divΦ.
- divΦ is bounded and supported in B, so by Cauchy–Schwarz |∫_B (u_j − c_j − W)·divΦ| ≤ (∫_B (u_j − c_j − W)²)^{1/2}(∫_B (divΦ)²)^{1/2} → 0.
- Hence −∫_B W·divΦ = lim_j −∫_B (u_j − c_j)·divΦ = lim_j −∫_B u_j·divΦ = lim_j ∫_B ∇u_j·Φ, using step 1 and ∫_B divΦ = 0.
- For every j, |∫_B ∇u_j·Φ| ≤ ∫_B ‖Du_j‖·|Φ| ≤ (∫_B ‖Du_j‖²)^{1/2}(∫_B |Φ|²)^{1/2} ≤ √E·(∫_B |Φ|²)^{1/2}. The bound passes to the limit.

4. (Energy on interior balls.) Let 0 < r < R.
- Choose χ_r ∈ C^∞(ℝⁿ) with 0 ≤ χ_r ≤ 1, χ_r ≡ 1 on B̆_r(0) and tsupport χ_r ⊆ closedBall(0, (r + R)/2) ⊆ B (a ContDiffBump centred at 0 with rIn = r, rOut = (r + R)/2).
- Put Φ_i := χ_r·∂_ih on B and Φ_i := 0 off B. Since h is C² on B, Φ_i is C¹ on B and vanishes on the open set ℝⁿ ∖ tsupport χ_r. So Φ ∈ 𝒱.
- ∇h·Φ = χ_r‖Dh‖² and |Φ|² = χ_r²‖Dh‖² ≤ χ_r‖Dh‖².
- Let X := ∫_B χ_r‖Dh‖². It is finite, because the integrand is continuous with compact support in B.
- Step 3 gives X ≤ √E·√X, hence X ≤ E (trivial if X = 0; otherwise divide by √X).
- Since χ_r = 1 on B̆_r(0) and the integrand is ≥ 0, ∫_{B̆_r(0)} ‖Dh‖² ≤ X ≤ E.

5. (Exhaustion.) ‖Dh‖² is continuous on B, hence a.e.-strongly measurable for volume.restrict B. Take r_k := R(1 − 1/(k + 1)) ↑ R. By monotone convergence for lower integrals, ∫⁻_B ‖Dh‖² = lim_k ∫⁻_{B̆_{r_k}(0)} ‖Dh‖² ≤ E < ∞. Hence ‖Dh‖² is integrable on B and ∫_B ‖Dh‖² ≤ E. ∎

Part 6 (proof of the statement = Lemma HA; Lemmas PI, RC, WL and EL are Parts 3, 4, 2 and 5).
Lemma HA (harmonic approximation; Simon 3.1). For every n ≥ 1 and every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with the following property. Let R₀ > 0 and let w : ℝⁿ → ℝ (ℝⁿ = Euclid n) be Lipschitz with ∫_{B̆_{R₀}(0)} ‖Dw‖² ≤ R₀ⁿ and |∫_{B̆_{R₀}(0)} Σ_i ∂_iw·∂_iζ| ≤ δR₀ⁿG for every C¹ compactly supported ζ : ℝⁿ → ℝ with tsupport ζ ⊆ B̆_{R₀}(0) and every G ∈ ℝ with ‖Dζ(v)‖ ≤ G for all v (Dw = fderiv ℝ w, ∂_iw = Dw(e_i), e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1). Then there is h : ℝⁿ → ℝ such that: h is C^m on B̆_{R₀}(0) for every m ∈ ℕ; Σ_i iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 h y ![e_i, e_i] = 0 for every y ∈ B̆_{R₀}(0); ‖Dh‖² is integrable on B̆_{R₀}(0) with ∫_{B̆_{R₀}(0)} ‖Dh‖² ≤ R₀ⁿ; and (h − w)² is integrable on B̆_{R₀}(0) with ∫_{B̆_{R₀}(0)} (h − w)² ≤ εR₀^{n+2}.
Proof of Lemma HA.
Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 5, Lemma 3.1 (Harmonic Approximation Lemma) and its printed proof, first for the unit ball (Part A below), then rescaled (Part B below). W^{1,2} is unavailable in the frozen Lean setting, so the proof is adapted as follows:
- the f_k are Lipschitz;
- the harmonicity of the L² limit comes from the distributional identity ∫WΔζ = 0 and Lemma WL, instead of from weak convergence of gradients;
- the energy bound for the limit comes from Lemma EL, instead of weak lower semicontinuity.
Lemmas used: PI (constant C_P), RC, WL and EL above.

Notation.
- B_ρ := B̆_ρ(0) and ω := Lⁿ(B_1).
- For Lipschitz u and C¹ ζ, ∇u·∇ζ := Σ_i Du(e_i)·Dζ(e_i). This is exactly the Lean integrand Σ_i fderiv ℝ u v (e_i) * fderiv ℝ ζ v (e_i).
- Δζ := Σ_i D²ζ(e_i, e_i) with D²ζ(y)(a, b) = iteratedFDeriv ℝ 2 ζ y ![a, b].
- H(w, R₀, δ) is the hypothesis of the statement: for every C¹ compactly supported ζ with tsupport ζ ⊆ B_{R₀} and every G with ‖Dζ(v)‖ ≤ G for all v, |∫_{B_{R₀}} ∇w·∇ζ| ≤ δR₀ⁿG.
- "h is admissible for (w, R₀, ε)" means: h is C^m on B_{R₀} for every m ∈ ℕ; Δh = 0 on B_{R₀}; ‖Dh‖² is integrable on B_{R₀} with ∫_{B_{R₀}} ‖Dh‖² ≤ R₀ⁿ; and (h − w)² is integrable on B_{R₀} with ∫_{B_{R₀}} (h − w)² ≤ εR₀^{n+2}.

Step 0 (integration by parts). Let u be Lipschitz and ζ ∈ C²(ℝⁿ) with compact support and tsupport ζ ⊆ B_1. Then ∫_{B_1} ∇u·∇ζ = −∫_{B_1} u·Δζ and ∫_{B_1} Δζ = 0.
Proof:
- g_i := Dζ(·)e_i is C¹ with compact support, hence Lipschitz.
- LipschitzWith.integral_lineDeriv_mul_eq with f := u, g := g_i, v := e_i gives ∫ lineDeriv ℝ u y e_i·g_i(y) dy = ∫ lineDeriv ℝ g_i y (−e_i)·u(y) dy = −∫ Dg_i(y)(e_i)·u(y) dy, and Dg_i(y)(e_i) = D²ζ(y)(e_i, e_i) (iteratedFDeriv_two_apply).
- For a.e. y, u is differentiable at y (Rademacher) and lineDeriv ℝ u y e_i = Du(y)e_i.
- Summing over i gives the first identity on ℝⁿ, and both integrands vanish outside tsupport ζ ⊆ B_1. With u ≡ 1 we get ∫_{B_1} Δζ = 0.

Part A (R₀ = 1). Claim A: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that every Lipschitz w with ∫_{B_1} ‖Dw‖² ≤ 1 and H(w, 1, δ) has an admissible h for (w, 1, ε).
A1. Suppose Claim A fails for some ε > 0. Then for each j ∈ ℕ, taking δ := 1/(j + 1), there is a Lipschitz w_j with ∫_{B_1} ‖Dw_j‖² ≤ 1 and H(w_j, 1, 1/(j + 1)) for which no admissible h for (w_j, 1, ε) exists.
A2. Let λ_j := ω^{−1}∫_{B_1} w_j and u_j := w_j − λ_j. Then u_j is Lipschitz and Du_j = Dw_j.
- By Lemma PI, ∫_{B_1} u_j² ≤ C_P∫_{B_1} ‖Dw_j‖² ≤ C_P.
- With M := max(C_P, 1), Lemma RC applies to (u_j). It gives a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ and W with MemLp W 2 on B_1 and ∫_{B_1} (u_{φ(j)} − W)² → 0.
A3. Let ζ ∈ C²(ℝⁿ) with compact support and tsupport ζ ⊆ B_1.
- ζ is C¹, and Dζ is continuous with compact support, so G_ζ := sup_v ‖Dζ(v)‖ < ∞.
- H(w_k, 1, 1/(k + 1)) with G = G_ζ gives |∫_{B_1} ∇w_k·∇ζ| ≤ G_ζ/(k + 1).
- By Step 0, ∫_{B_1} u_k·Δζ = ∫_{B_1} w_k·Δζ − λ_k∫_{B_1} Δζ = −∫_{B_1} ∇w_k·∇ζ. Hence |∫_{B_1} u_{φ(j)}·Δζ| ≤ G_ζ/(φ(j) + 1) → 0.
- Δζ is bounded, so by Cauchy–Schwarz |∫_{B_1} (u_{φ(j)} − W)·Δζ| ≤ (∫_{B_1} (u_{φ(j)} − W)²)^{1/2}(∫_{B_1} (Δζ)²)^{1/2} → 0.
- Therefore ∫_{B_1} W·Δζ = 0.
W is integrable on B_1 (it is L² on a set of finite measure). So Lemma WL with R = 1 gives h̃ that is C^m on B_1 for every m, with Δh̃ = 0 on B_1 and h̃ = W a.e. on B_1.
A4. Apply Lemma EL with R = 1, E = 1, the Lipschitz functions w_{φ(j)}, the constants c_j := λ_{φ(j)}, the function W, and h := h̃ (C² on B_1). Its hypotheses hold: ∫_{B_1} ‖Dw_{φ(j)}‖² ≤ 1, and ∫_{B_1} (w_{φ(j)} − λ_{φ(j)} − W)² = ∫_{B_1} (u_{φ(j)} − W)² → 0. Hence ‖Dh̃‖² is integrable on B_1 and ∫_{B_1} ‖Dh̃‖² ≤ 1.
A5. Choose j with ∫_{B_1} (u_{φ(j)} − W)² ≤ ε, and put h := h̃ + λ_{φ(j)}.
- Adding a constant changes no derivative of order ≥ 1. So on B_1, h is C^m for every m, Dh = Dh̃, D²h = D²h̃, Δh = 0, and ‖Dh‖² is integrable with ∫_{B_1} ‖Dh‖² ≤ 1 = 1ⁿ.
- A.e. on B_1, h − w_{φ(j)} = h̃ − u_{φ(j)} = W − u_{φ(j)}. So (h − w_{φ(j)})² is integrable on B_1 (W ∈ L² and u_{φ(j)} is bounded on B_1), and ∫_{B_1} (h − w_{φ(j)})² ≤ ε = ε·1^{n+2}.
Thus h is admissible for (w_{φ(j)}, 1, ε), contradicting A1 for the index φ(j). This proves Claim A.

Part B (scaling). Given ε > 0, let δ be the constant of Claim A for this ε. Let R₀ > 0 and let w be Lipschitz with ∫_{B_{R₀}} ‖Dw‖² ≤ R₀ⁿ and H(w, R₀, δ).
B1. Put w₁(y) := R₀^{−1}w(R₀y). It is Lipschitz.
- Dw₁(y) = Dw(R₀y) for every y. If w is differentiable at R₀y this is the chain rule. Otherwise w₁ is not differentiable at y either, because w = R₀w₁(·/R₀), and both fderivs are 0.
- Change of variables x = R₀y: Measure.setIntegral_comp_smul_of_pos with finrank = n and R₀·B_1 = B_{R₀} (and Measure.map_addHaar_smul for lower integrals) give ∫_{B_1} F(R₀y) dy = R₀^{−n}∫_{B_{R₀}} F for F integrable on B_{R₀} or F ≥ 0 measurable. Integrability transfers in both directions.
- So ∫_{B_1} ‖Dw₁‖² = R₀^{−n}∫_{B_{R₀}} ‖Dw‖² ≤ 1.
B2. H(w₁, 1, δ) holds. Let ζ₁ be C¹ with compact support and tsupport ζ₁ ⊆ B_1, and let G satisfy ‖Dζ₁(v)‖ ≤ G for all v.
- Put ζ(x) := R₀ζ₁(x/R₀). ζ is C¹ with compact support, tsupport ζ = R₀·tsupport ζ₁ ⊆ B_{R₀}, and Dζ(x) = Dζ₁(x/R₀), so ‖Dζ(x)‖ ≤ G.
- By H(w, R₀, δ), |∫_{B_{R₀}} ∇w·∇ζ| ≤ δR₀ⁿG.
- By B1 and the change of variables, ∫_{B_{R₀}} ∇w·∇ζ = ∫_{B_{R₀}} Σ_i Dw(x)e_i·Dζ₁(x/R₀)e_i dx = R₀ⁿ∫_{B_1} Σ_i Dw(R₀y)e_i·Dζ₁(y)e_i dy = R₀ⁿ∫_{B_1} ∇w₁·∇ζ₁.
Hence |∫_{B_1} ∇w₁·∇ζ₁| ≤ δG.
B3. By Claim A there is h₁ admissible for (w₁, 1, ε). Put h(x) := R₀h₁(x/R₀).
- h is C^m on B_{R₀} for every m, since x ↦ x/R₀ is linear and maps B_{R₀} onto B_1.
- Dh(x) = Dh₁(x/R₀) and D²h(x)(a, b) = R₀^{−1}D²h₁(x/R₀)(a, b). So Δh(x) = R₀^{−1}Δh₁(x/R₀) = 0 on B_{R₀}.
- By the change of variables of B1, ‖Dh‖² is integrable on B_{R₀} and ∫_{B_{R₀}} ‖Dh‖² = R₀ⁿ∫_{B_1} ‖Dh₁‖² ≤ R₀ⁿ.
- Since h(x) − w(x) = R₀(h₁ − w₁)(x/R₀), (h − w)² is integrable on B_{R₀} and ∫_{B_{R₀}} (h − w)² = R₀²·R₀ⁿ∫_{B_1} (h₁ − w₁)² ≤ εR₀^{n+2}.
So h has every property required by the statement, with a δ that depends only on n and ε. ∎
proof_key_steps: Parts 1–2 (Lemmas MV and WL). Let W be in L¹(B) with ∫_B WΔζ = 0 for every C² test function ζ supported in B. Each radial mollification W_ε is harmonic on B̆_{R−ε}(0). The radial mean value property and ρ_ε ⋆ ρ_δ = ρ_δ ⋆ ρ_ε make W_ε(x) independent of ε. So the W_ε glue to a function harmonic on B, and Lebesgue differentiation shows it equals W almost everywhere.
Part 3 (Lemma PI). For Lipschitz u, ∫_{B_1}(u − ū)² ≤ 2^{n+2}∫_{B_1}‖Du‖². The proof uses FTC on almost every segment, Cauchy–Schwarz, and a change of variables based on convexity of the ball.

Part 4 (Lemma RC). A sequence of Lipschitz functions with uniformly bounded L²(B_1) norm and Dirichlet energy has a subsequence converging in L²(B_1). Interior mollification and Arzelà–Ascoli on K_s control the interior. Rays and dilations give the boundary-layer bound ∫_{A_s}u² ≤ 2^{n+3}s(∫u² + ∫‖Du‖²). The family is therefore totally bounded in the complete space L², so a subsequence converges.

Part 5 (Lemma EL). Suppose u_j − c_j → W in L²(B), and h is a C² function equal to W almost everywhere. Then ∫_B‖Dh‖² ≤ E. The proof integrates by parts against C¹_c vector fields to get a duality bound. Testing with Φ = χ_r∇h bounds the energy on each interior ball, and exhaustion finishes.

Part 6A (R₀ = 1), by contradiction. Take counterexamples w_j for δ = 1/(j + 1) and subtract their means λ_j. PI and RC give an L² limit W. Step 0 and the hypothesis give ∫WΔζ = 0. WL gives a harmonic h̃ with h̃ = W a.e., and EL gives ∫‖Dh̃‖² ≤ 1. Then h̃ + λ_{φ(j)} is admissible for w_{φ(j)}, a contradiction.

Part 6B (scaling). Set w₁(y) = R₀^{−1}w(R₀y), ζ(x) = R₀ζ₁(x/R₀) and h(x) = R₀h₁(x/R₀). These transfer the hypotheses from B_{R₀} to B_1 and the conclusions back. In particular ∫_{B_{R₀}}(h − w)² = R₀^{n+2}∫_{B_1}(h₁ − w₁)² ≤ εR₀^{n+2}, and δ depends only on n and ε.
